edge_357.relationship: Guha treats colonial peasant insurgency as deliberate political action and consciousness

edge_386.relationship: Spivak and Stoler question different limits of Foucault’s accounts of power
edge_386.evidence_note: Spivak’s primary essay addresses representation and labor; Stoler’s publisher description identifies empire and race. Their criticisms coexist with productive theoretical use.

edge_389.relationship: Spivak questions the gendered recovery of an autonomous subaltern subject
edge_389.evidence_note: The primary Guha discussion and gender argument supply a bounded intervention; her critique does not equate subalternity with literal voicelessness.

edge_604.relationship: Guha challenges colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism in Indian historiography
edge_604.evidence_note: The checked 1982 essay distinguishes popular political domains while allowing overlap and variable regional positions. Its argument is not a denial of all national histories or a claim that popular politics is uniformly autonomous.

nationaltradition.label: National & imperial narratives
nationaltradition.description: National and imperial histories join source work to competing accounts of peoples, states, liberty and civilization. Michelet, Macaulay and Bancroft differ in method and purpose; colonial hierarchies, liberation histories and critiques of nationalist exclusions remain in tension.
nationaltradition.representative_figures_and_works: A broad context of historical production, not one school: nation-building, colonial institutions, and resistance generate different and often conflicting projects.

representative_people.context: Interweaves archives, geography, cultural life and a self-forming French people. The 1869 preface admires and disputes Thierry, credits Vico and reflects on the historian’s participation. His revolutionary history later becomes Barthes’s narrative example.
representative_people.works: Histoire de France (1833–1867), preface of 1869; Histoire de la Révolution française (1847–1853); later analysis in Barthes (1968)

representative_people.context: Connects constitutional settlement, commerce, empire and everyday manners while acknowledging crimes and failures. His education minute argues for a hierarchy of knowledge and English-trained imperial intermediaries. Distinct from Catharine Macaulay.
representative_people.works: The History of England from the Accession of James II, volume I, chapter I; “Minute on Indian Education” (2 February 1835)

representative_people.context: Combines comparative documentary criticism with a story of liberty developing from colonial institutions. His professed impartiality does not establish equal representation of all inhabitants.
representative_people.works: History of the United States / History of the Colonization of the United States, volume I (first-edition preface 1834; consulted 17th edition 1859)

representative_people.context: Uses Michelet and Thierry to question narrative transparency and examine how writing signifies historical reality. These readings do not dismiss all national histories or independently refute their factual claims.
representative_people.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Michelet admires his national narrative while criticizing an explanatory commitment to the permanence of races; this is an attributed reception, not a reading of Thierry’s original work.

representative_people.context: Michelet names his account of humanity making itself as a central resource; this does not derive all national history from Vico.

nationaltradition.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not a single national or imperial doctrine. Cultural and documentary inquiry coexist with narratives of progress. Colonial policy, anticolonial histories, subaltern criticism and collective African projects have different aims; no universal nationalist origin or automatic emancipation is implied.

strands.title: National narratives and the appearance of reality
strands.focus: Michelet’s revolutionary history becomes an object of Barthes’s analysis of detail and signification; this later reading is distinguished from original research and bibliography.
strands.works: Histoire de la Révolution française (1847–1853); Barthes (1967–1968)

strands.title: Reconstructing a people and its historical life

strands.title: Constitutional settlement, commerce and empire
strands.focus: Macaulay’s prospectus links liberties and prosperity to imperial power but also names crimes, Irish oppression and failures. Manners and material life form part of his project.
strands.works: History of England, volume I, chapter I opening

strands.title: Documentary criticism and republican beginnings
strands.focus: Bancroft seeks contemporary accounts and comparison of witnesses while reading early institutions as the beginnings of national liberty.
strands.works: Volume I prefaces (1834, 1838), consulted 1859 edition

strands.title: Historical authority and imperial education
strands.focus: Macaulay’s minute connects public funding, language hierarchy and intermediary elites. The stated policy argument does not prove its implementation or the inferiority of other knowledge traditions.

strands.title: Different critiques of imperial narratives
strands.focus: James, Williams and Césaire contest empire through revolutionary agency, economic explanation and a critique of civilizing claims. Their arguments do not collapse into one national-liberation doctrine.
strands.works: The Black Jacobins (1938); Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Discourse on Colonialism (1950/1955)

strands.title: Nationalist exclusions and alternative scales

strands.title: Historical individuality and national statehood
strands.focus: Meinecke’s historical philosophy crosses into national narration. The connection between particular development and state power requires scrutiny rather than acceptance as an organic necessity.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); The Chartists (1984); Elementary Aspects (1983)

strands.title: Rights movements and political inclusion
strands.focus: Sustained organization for women’s rights is part of political history; it is not merely an appendix to histories of officeholders.
strands.works: Century of Struggle (1959)

strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.
strands.works: The Contentious French (1986); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities
strands.focus: Hunt uses Geertz in an analysis of revolutionary authority and joins symbolic practices with the sociology of political actors.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984)

strands.title: Diplomacy, conflict and expansion
strands.focus: Narrative accounts of political choices differ from Williams’s interpretation of ideology, political economy and American expansion; diplomatic history contains disagreement.
strands.works: The Guns of August (1962); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

strands.title: Radical milieus, hostile sources and disputed labels
strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); “On the Rant” and correspondence (1987)

strands.title: Local government, record production and representation
strands.focus: Cam’s inquiry connects the making of records, local courts and parliamentary representation. Documentary criticism and inferences about ordinary lives remain distinct tasks.
strands.works: Cam, Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921), Liberties and Communities (1944), “Stubbs Seventy Years after” (1948)

strands.title: Narrative, motives and contemporary uncertainty
strands.focus: Wedgwood reconstructs decisions without giving actors knowledge of their outcome. Woolrych also asks what this approach leaves unexplained about allegiance and regional differences.
strands.works: The King’s Peace (1955); The King’s War (1958), prefaces discussed by Woolrych (1998)

strands.title: Narrative synthesis and specialist collaboration
strands.focus: Tuchman’s account of producing A Distant Mirror identifies research, medieval advice and editing. These contributions support a synthesis whose event selection and explanatory claims remain open to criticism.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), acknowledgments and foreword

strands.title: Political ideas in different social situations
strands.focus: Wood questions applying Namier’s skepticism about ideas to revolutionary America. His reading of Bailyn connects changing beliefs with social circumstances and unintended outcomes; it does not make all political action a deliberate pursuit of abstract principles.
strands.works: Namier, “Human Nature in Politics” (1955/2000); Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality” (1966/1968), 69–78

strands.title: Press freedom and institutional dependence
strands.focus: Goldman traces how municipal protection, financing and censorship shaped political printing. Public controversy emerged through conflicts among editors and authorities, rather than automatically following a declaration of press freedom.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 10–15

strands.title: Public spaces and competing explanations
strands.focus: Goldman uses a plural account of public spaces. Sábato asks whether the collection’s cultural emphasis loses explanatory specificity and overlooks republican currents or differences among cases, while recognizing its comparative value.
strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

coverage.basis: Reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment. Later work is not yet surveyed for this entry; selected later interventions, where present, are dated individually.

subaltern.label: Subaltern Studies
subaltern.description: Critiques colonial and elite nationalist histories; begins with subordinate groups’ politics and develops debates over representation and historical knowledge.
subaltern.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha; Shahid Amin; Dipesh Chakrabarty. Neither all South Asian history nor all postcolonial thought.

representative_people.context: Proposes an autonomous domain of popular politics while recognizing overlap with elites and variable regional social positions.
representative_people.works: “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983)

representative_people.context: Combines judicial archives and local interviews to examine peasant politics and competing national memories.
representative_people.works: Event, Metaphor, Memory: Chauri Chaura, 1922–1992 (1995)

representative_people.context: Revises universalizing class narratives through Bengal labor; later investigates historians’ translations of subordinate pasts.
representative_people.works: Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (1997); Provincializing Europe (2000)

representative_people.context: Addresses the relationship between colonial nationalism and cultural difference within a changing collective.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Critically engages Guha’s autonomy claim and the gendered limits of recovering subaltern consciousness.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

representative_people.context: Historicizes communalism as a category and explores contested political communities.
representative_people.works: The Construction of Communalism in Colonial North India (1990)

representative_people.context: Examines science as both imperial authority and a resource for national emancipation.
representative_people.works: Another Reason: Science and the Imagination of Modern India (1999)

representative_people.context: Credits early research while contesting later priorities and identifying tensions within the initial project.
representative_people.works: “The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies,” in Writing Social History (1997)

representative_people.context: Recognizes Chakrabarty’s theoretical intervention while questioning static cultural categories and the treatment of gender.
representative_people.works: Review of Rethinking Working Class History (1990), 96–99

representative_people.context: Wrote the foreword to the 1988 Selected Subaltern Studies anthology edited by Guha and Spivak. This is a documented editorial contribution; it does not establish founding, collective membership or the direction of theoretical borrowing.
representative_people.works: Foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988)

subaltern.scope_note: The collective changes across time; subordinate agency, colonial archives, and representation must not become a single unchanging postcolonial theory. Guha’s autonomy thesis, Spivak’s representation problem and Sarkar’s internal criticism are not interchangeable. Religion, gender, labor, local memory and colonial knowledge remain distinct questions; the present roster is geographically selective.

strands.title: Popular politics and elite historiography
strands.focus: Autonomy is an argued distinction, with interaction and regional variation built into the early statement.
strands.works: Guha (1982); Elementary Aspects (1983)

strands.title: Local events, archives and remembrance
strands.focus: Different records and recollections complicate national narratives of Chauri Chaura.
strands.works: Event, Metaphor, Memory (1995)

strands.title: Labor and historical difference
strands.focus: Bengal’s jute workers prompt criticism of universal class narratives that leave culture residual.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989)

strands.title: Historical translation and its limits
strands.focus: Religious accounts of agency pose a problem for the secular historian’s narration.
strands.works: “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (1997)

strands.title: Nation, community and colonial categories
strands.focus: Nationalism and communalism receive distinct historical critiques; political communities are not timeless givens.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993); The Construction of Communalism (1990)

strands.title: Gender and the recovery of consciousness
strands.focus: Representation remains necessary and difficult; adding women to a list does not settle the problem.
strands.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

strands.title: Science and national imagination
strands.focus: Scientific reason acquires different political uses under empire and nationalism.
strands.works: Another Reason (1999)

strands.title: Disputing the project’s changing priorities
strands.focus: Sarkar defends research into subordinate social groups while questioning community-centered explanations.
strands.works: “The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies” (1997)

coverage.basis: Reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment. Later work is not yet surveyed for this entry; selected later interventions, where present, are dated individually.

post.label: Postcolonial history / critique
post.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
post.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000). Gyan Prakash: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); Stuart Hall: “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’?” (1996); Paul Gilroy: The Black Atlantic (1993).

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

representative_people.context: Tests European social-science categories against South Asian political histories while retaining their critical uses.
representative_people.works: Provincializing Europe (2000)

representative_people.context: Develops colonial historical difference through an explicit disagreement with Anderson.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines ambivalence, mimicry and hybrid cultural production; these concepts are debated interpretations.
representative_people.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

representative_people.context: Criticizes homogenizing accounts of women and develops historically situated feminist solidarity.
representative_people.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

representative_people.context: Reworks Foucault through colonial archives, race and sexuality.
representative_people.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996)

representative_people.context: His criticism of idealized and denigrating images of India supplies a specific resource for Guha’s environmental argument. Original article remains to be distinguished from its documented reception.
representative_people.works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), especially442, through Guha (1989)

representative_people.context: Historian whose essays set out postcolonial historiography from Indian historiography and read Subaltern Studies as postcolonial criticism. His Subaltern Studies context remains distinct.
representative_people.works: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); “Subaltern Studies as Postcolonial Criticism” (1994)

representative_people.context: Cultural theorist whose essays on diasporic identity and on the category of the “post-colonial” are standard resources in postcolonial critique. His cultural-studies context remains separate.
representative_people.works: “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” (1990); “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’? Thinking at the Limit” (1996)

representative_people.context: The Black Atlantic criticizes national and racial closure and reads modernity through the Black Atlantic; a standard postcolonial and diaspora text for historians. His Atlantic and diaspora contexts remain.
representative_people.works: The Black Atlantic (1993)

representative_people.context: Coedited Tensions of Empire with Ann Laura Stoler (1997) and coauthored its opening research-agenda chapter. The publisher describes a historical and anthropological inquiry into relations between metropole and colony and changing categories of colonial rule. This contextual inclusion does not identify Cooper as an adherent of every postcolonial theory; his later criticisms require a separate dated claim.
representative_people.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), coedited with Ann Laura Stoler; opening chapter, “Between Metropole and Colony: Rethinking a Research Agenda”

post.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

strands.title: Imperial knowledge and cultural authority
strands.focus: Texts acquire authority through institutions and citation; individual writers remain consequential.
strands.works: Orientalism (1978)

strands.title: Representation and intellectual responsibility
strands.focus: Speaking for others and depicting them pose connected political problems.
strands.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

strands.title: Provincializing historical categories
strands.focus: Critique works through inherited concepts without treating Europe as every society’s model.
strands.works: Provincializing Europe (2000)

strands.title: Colonial nationalism and difference
strands.focus: Bengal supplies the setting for a disputed account of cultural autonomy and political modernity.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

strands.title: Mimicry, ambivalence and hybridity
strands.focus: Colonial authority and identification are examined through unstable cultural meanings.
strands.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

strands.title: Feminist difference and coalition
strands.focus: Neither women’s situations nor feminist scholarship form a single homogeneous subject.
strands.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984/1991)

strands.title: Race, sexuality and colonial archives
strands.focus: Empire becomes part of the history of European bourgeois sexuality.
strands.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

strands.title: Critiquing the romanticized East
strands.focus: Guha applies Inden’s critique of hostile and admiring Orientalist images to environmental appropriations of Asian traditions. This documents a particular reception, without making those traditions homogeneous or certifying Inden’s whole argument.
strands.works: Inden (1986), quoted and discussed by Guha (1989),77–78/note9

strands.title: Metropole and colony in a shared research agenda
strands.focus: Cooper and Stoler’s 1997 edited collection supplies a contextual reading on connections between imperial centres and colonial settings and the historical formation of categories of rule. This is the publisher’s description and contents, not a passage-level check or a claim that one programme defines postcolonial history.
strands.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), especially the opening chapter credited to Stoler and Cooper
